props.title: Christmas in the Heartland

sections.content: **Christmas in the Heartland (2017)** (2017) fits into the well-worn "trading places" holiday subgenre pioneered by The Parent Trap (1961). Following two teens who switch identities during a chance airport meeting, it echoes elements of It Takes Two (1995) and Model Behavior (2000), but with a distinctly rural American Christmas setting. While not breaking new ground, it joins the wave of heartland-focused holiday films like Christmas with the Kranks (2004) that emphasize traditional family values and small-town charm.

sections.content: The film leans heavily into familiar holiday movie tropes established by classics like **Miracle on 34th Street** (1947) and **White Christmas** (1954) - the importance of family connections, rediscovering Christmas spirit, and the magic of the season bringing people together. Director Justin Ward attempts to modernize these themes for contemporary audiences while maintaining the wholesome appeal that defines Hallmark-style holiday entertainment.

What sets **Christmas in the Heartland** (2017) apart is its emphasis on rural American Christmas traditions, following a trend seen in films like **Sweet Home Alabama** (2002) and **Hope Floats** (1998) that romanticize small-town life. The film's portrayal of heartland values mirrors similar holiday offerings like Christmas on the Range (2019) and **A Country Christmas Story** (2013). SUBHEAD: Modern Identity-Swap Holiday Films

sections.content: The identity-swap premise has evolved significantly since The Parent Trap (1961), with films like **Monte Carlo** (2011) and **The Princess Switch** (2018) adding modern twists to the formula. **Christmas in the Heartland** (2017) follows this tradition while incorporating elements of fish-out-of-water comedy seen in holiday classics like **Elf** (2003) and contemporary offerings like **A Princess for Christmas** (2011).
